t: In Europe and North America the movement grew from campaigns against the smoke of the Industrial Revolution and from the defence of countryside, forests and wildlife in the 19th century.
From the 1960s it campaigned against nuclear weapons and nuclear power, then acid rain, ozone depletion and deforestation, and most recently climate change.
It is an international movement of many organisations and approaches, not always united in its goals, and has faced critics who see it as radical and misguided.
dyk: The first permanent, large-scale forest conservation programme in the world was introduced in British India in 1855 under Governor-General Lord Dalhousie, a model that soon spread to other colonies and to the United States.
ev: The Madras Board of Revenue begins state forest conservation under the botanist Alexander Gibson
The Commons Preservation Society is founded in Britain to defend the countryside against industrialisation
John Muir founds the Sierra Club in the United States
Britain passes the Clean Air Act after the Great Smog of 1952 in London
The international environmental conference in Stockholm is held
The Chipko movement begins in India
The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development meets in Rio de Janeiro

f.where: worldwide: early centres in Britain, British India and Burma, and the United States; later movements in Germany, Spain, India, China, South Korea, Taiwan, Brazil and the rest of Latin America, the Arab world and South Africa
f.period: Romantic roots and smoke abatement in the 19th century; state forest conservation in British India from 1842 and 1855; conservation and amenity societies in Britain from 1865 and in the United States from the late 19th century; the contemporary movement from the 1960s; international conferences in Stockholm (1972) and Rio de Janeiro (1992); environmental justice, indigenous rights and the climate crisis in recent decades
f.figures: Robert Hunter, Octavia Hill and Hardwicke Rawnsley, founders of the National Trust; John Ruskin; Sir William Blake Richmond of the Coal Smoke Abatement Society; the zoologist Alfred Newton; the foresters Alexander Gibson, Hugh Cleghorn and Dietrich Brandis; Henry David Thoreau, author of Walden; John Muir, founder of the Sierra Club; Rachel Carson, author of Silent Spring; Senator Gaylord Nelson; Chandi Prasad Bhatt in India
f.outcome: nature protection, clean air and clean water laws, among them Britain’s Clean Air Act 1956 and the United States’ Clean Water, Clean Air and Endangered Species Acts of the 1970s; the National Trust, national parks and state forest departments; a movement still active and not always united, now much concerned with climate change
